title: Is this trade worth it?
objectives: Count what a capture actually wins before playing it
Recognize when a tempting capture is really a losing trade

steps.text: Not every capture wins material. Before you take a piece, count: what do you win, and what can they win back? If the exchange loses you more than it gains, it's a bad trade — even though the move itself is perfectly legal.

steps.prompt: Your queen can capture on d4 or g4. Only one of these actually wins material — play that one.

hints.text: One of the two captures is defended, and one isn't. Check both before choosing.
The pawn on d4 is defended by the pawn on e5 — capturing it just loses your queen.
Qxg4 wins the knight for free — nothing defends g4.

feedback.default: That capture doesn't win material. Count what defends each target before you take it — one of these two is a trap.

steps.successExplanation: Qxg4 wins the knight for free — nothing defends g4. Qxd4 would have lost the queen for a single pawn, since the pawn on e5 recaptures immediately.

steps.prompt: Your bishop (worth about 3 points) attacks an enemy knight (also worth about 3) that's defended by a pawn. What actually happens if you capture it?
options: You win a knight for free
You trade your bishop for their knight — roughly even material
You lose your bishop for nothing

feedback.default: That's not what a defended, equal-value capture produces. Work out what happens after the recapture: you gain the knight, then lose the bishop.

steps.successExplanation: Right — you win the knight, they recapture with the pawn and win your bishop back. Roughly equal value changed hands; it's a trade, not a win.

steps.summary: Before capturing, count what you actually get and what you can lose back. A capture that starts an even or losing exchange isn't automatically good — look for the target that's genuinely undefended, or worth more than what you're giving up.
